title: Do not borrow a name when you need a position.
dek: In Chapter 11 of Positioning, Al Ries and Jack Trout show how a familiar name can carry inherited recognition while failing to give a new offer a distinct place in the mind. The discipline is to separate borrowed equity from a position the buyer can actually remember.

canon.heading: Inherited recognition is not a free position.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 11, "The Free-Ride Trap," from Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning on PDF pages 85-90. Study how a name can carry the memory of an earlier offer while weakening the new offer's ability to occupy a distinct mental slot.
canon.readerIntro: Read this as an audit of borrowed meaning. Mark where a familiar name helps a new offer get noticed, where it creates confusion about the category or promise, and where the authors distinguish recognition from a defensible position. Then audit one extension or sub-brand you know. Stop at PDF page 90.

blocks.label: 01 / Familiarity can disguise strategic debt
paragraphs: A well-known name appears to offer a shortcut into the market, but its associations were earned by an earlier product, category, or promise.
Ask what the new offer receives immediately and what it must spend effort explaining because the inherited meaning points somewhere else.

blocks.label: 02 / Borrowed equity is not a new position
paragraphs: Recognition may win the first glance without telling the prospect what this particular offer stands for. The mental handle has to identify the new choice, not merely recall the old one.
Notice the difference between entering memory and occupying a useful place inside it.

blocks.label: 03 / The name changes the comparison frame
paragraphs: A borrowed name can force the new offer to be judged against the parent brand or its established competitors, even when the intended strategy requires a different comparison.
Study which comparison the name makes automatic and whether that comparison helps the buyer understand the offer.

blocks.label: 04 / Make the extension earn its own meaning
paragraphs: The practical question is not whether a name is famous. It is whether the new offer can build a clear, credible association that survives once the inherited familiarity fades.
Look for the cost of asking one name to carry incompatible promises, audiences, or categories.

blocks.label: 05 / Audit one borrowed position
paragraphs: Choose one extension, sub-brand, or product family. Write the inherited association, the new promise, and the single position the buyer should remember.
Stop with one recommendation: keep the name, narrow the promise, or create a clearer handle for the new offer.

closeReading: What does the familiar name give the new offer immediately, and what does it fail to communicate?
Where does recognition become confused with a distinct position?
Which comparison does the inherited name make automatic for the prospect?
Choose one extension or sub-brand. What association does it inherit, and what new promise is it trying to make?
Should the offer keep its name, narrow its promise, or create a clearer handle? What would the buyer remember?

principle.heading: Make the new offer earn its own mental slot.
principle.body: A familiar name can reduce the cost of being noticed, but it cannot substitute for a clear position. Separate inherited recognition from the promise the buyer should attach to this offer.
principle.example: A trusted cleaning brand that launches a premium home-security service may gain an initial glance from the parent name, but the buyer still needs a distinct reason to remember the new offer: what category it belongs to, what risk it removes, and why this name is credible there.
principle.practice: Pick one brand extension. Write the parent brand's inherited meaning, the extension's intended category, and the one association it should own. If those three do not align, rewrite the promise or recommend a clearer name.

output.heading: Borrow attention carefully; build meaning deliberately.
output.body: Use familiarity to earn a first look, then give the new offer a position that can be remembered without the parent brand doing all the work.

fieldNotes.title: ChatGPT adds privacy as a visible product boundary
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI added Locked Chats to ChatGPT, letting users protect selected conversations with a PIN or device biometrics and place them in a separate section. The feature does not change retention, encryption, or model-improvement settings.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product is making a familiar name carry a more specific promise: not simply private, but visibly separated at the moment another person may use the device. The boundary is useful because it tells the user what protection exists and what it does not change.
fieldNotes.watch: When a product inherits broad trust, look for the concrete boundary that makes the new promise memorable, and state the limits beside the benefit.

fieldNotes.title: Meta’s Muse is buying reach, then testing retention
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reports that Meta’s Muse reached 10.9 million downloads in its first 40 days, with 39% of Meta’s advertising spend allocated to the app in October. Sensor Tower data also showed higher seven- and fourteen-day retention than the cited AI competitors.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A famous parent can accelerate discovery, but the new offer still has to earn a distinct reason to remain in the user’s routine. Distribution creates the first look; retention tests whether the product has built its own position.
fieldNotes.watch: Separate the inherited reach of a platform or parent brand from the repeat behavior the new product can generate on its own.

fieldNotes.title: Google is carrying personal context into the car
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google began rolling out Personal Intelligence with Gemini in Android Auto, connecting opted-in users’ Gmail, Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Search history, and other services so the assistant can answer contextual questions while driving.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The feature is not only a new assistant capability; it is a new comparison frame for the car interface. Google is asking the vehicle to be understood as another doorway into a personal ecosystem, while the opt-in and app controls define the trust boundary.
fieldNotes.watch: When extending a familiar service into a new context, ask whether the inherited meaning clarifies the job or silently expands the user’s exposure.

fieldNotes.title: Marriott turns a loyalty program into a travel relationship
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Marketing Dive reports that Marriott Bonvoy’s new global platform positions the program as a lifelong travel partner rather than only a loyalty program. Creators produced campaign assets across 10 countries, 23 destinations, and 14 hotel brands in four weeks.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The campaign gives a broad inherited name a more specific emotional and operational role: showing up across real journeys. The creator system is valuable because it translates the promise into local scenes instead of asking one polished asset to carry every market.
fieldNotes.watch: For a broad platform or loyalty brand, identify the repeated situation in which the promise becomes visible and let local execution prove the same position.

tweets.title: A startup wins when the new physics force a new story
tweets.summary: This is worth keeping because it treats narrative as part of the operating system, not decoration. A strange technical or market bet has to become desirable before incumbents copy it, and the company has to keep moving fast enough that the story remains attached to real progress.
